title: Millikan's Oil-Drop Lab
summary: Tune the voltage until a charged oil drop hovers, measure its charge, and discover that charge comes in whole units of e.
subject: physics
learningOutcome: After winning, the student can balance a drop to measure its charge, count its electrons, find the unit of charge from data, and tell a possible charge from an impossible one.

levels.title: Hold the drop
levels.adds: Baseline: tune each drop to hover, read its charge from the lab, and work out how many electrons it carries.
hints: A drop hovers when the upward electric force equals its weight. Raise the voltage if it falls, lower it if it rises.
Fine-tune with the small buttons, then hold it steady for a second before you record.
Each electron carries e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, so the number of electrons is the drop's charge divided by e.

levels.title: Find the unit
levels.adds: New idea: e is not given. Measure several drops and find the unit that all the charges are whole multiples of.
hints: Every measured charge is a whole number of the same basic unit, give or take your tuning error.
Compare the charges: look for the biggest value that goes into all of them a whole number of times.
If your drops could all be multiples of 2e, you have not yet measured one that rules that out. Measure another drop.

levels.title: Impure samples
levels.adds: New idea: with e known, spot the drops whose charge cannot be real, because charge only comes in whole multiples of e.
hints: Divide each measured charge by e. A real drop gives a number very close to a whole number.
Your tuning is only accurate to a few percent, so allow a little slack around a whole number.
A reading near a half, like 2.5 or 4.5, cannot be a whole number of electrons: that sample is impure.

misconceptions: Charge can take any value at the atomic scale
The smallest measured charge must be the unit of charge
A measured value close to a half-integer is just noise
